newsitem.title: UK: Chronology of the exchange rate mechanism detailed.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of the exchange rate mechanism detailed.

text.p: The exchange rate mechanism (ERM) allows currencies to fluctuate within 15 percent bands either side of their fixed central rates, which is the case for all members except the German mark and Dutch guilder. The mark and guilder maintained 2.25 percent bands when the ERM was reshaped on August 1, 1993.
The system was subject to a number of crises in 1992 and 1993 revamp but since it has undergone a period of calm with limits not being tested by the markets.
The following is a chronology of the ERM:
March, 1979 - ERM formed. Mark, French franc, Belgian franc, Dutch guilder, Danish crown and Irish punt join with 2.25 percent bands. Italian lira joins with six pct bands.
Sept, 1979 - First change to ERM parities, mark revalued by two percent.
March, 1983 - French franc devalued for third time in two years amid balance of payments crisis.
April 7, 1986 - Last independent French franc devaluation.
Jan 12, 1987 - Mark and guilder revalued by three percentin ERM. Belgian franc and Danish crown revalued by 2 percent.

Sept 12, 1987 - Basle-Nyborg agreement grants central banks credit lines to finance intervention within permitted currency bands, or intra-marginal intervention, but lays emphasis in interest rate differentials to defend currencies.
April 17, 1989 - Delors Report outlines three-stage plan for European monetary union.
June 12, 1989 - Spanish peseta joins ERM, six percent bands.
Jan 8, 1990 - Italian lira devalues central rate by 3.7 percent, moves to 2.25 percent bands from six percent bands.
April 23, 1990 - West Germany offers one-for-one conversion between West German and East German marks for savings and wages to certain limits, effective from July 1.
Oct 8, 1990 - UK joins ERM with 2.95-marks central rate and six percent bands.
Dec 10, 1991 - European Union heads of government agree to the Treaty on European Union in Dutch town of Maastricht and pave the way for the creation of a single EU currency by 1999.
Feb 7, 1992 - Maastricht Treaty signed by EU finance and foreign ministers.
June 2, 1992 - Danes vote no to the Maastricht treaty, with 50.7 percent against. Markets question plan for single currency.
June 3, 1992 - French President Francois Mitterrand announces France will hold a referendum on Maastricht in the autumn.
July 16, 1992 - German Bundesbank announces 0.75 percentage point rise in its discount rate to a record 8.75 percent, boosting the mark further against th dollar and other European currencies.
June 19, 1992 - Ireland votes in favour of Maastricht, with 68.7 percent in favour.
Sept 3, 1992 - UK treasury borrows 16 billion European currency units to defned the pound within ERM
Sept 4, 1992 - Italy raises discount and Lombard rates by 1.75 percentage points each to defend lira in ERM.
Sept 5, 1992 - EC finance ministers, meeting under pressure in Bath, England, stress they have no plans for ERM realignment.
Sept 8, 1992 - Turmoil on European markets sweeps north as Finland severs the markka's link to the European Currency Unit and allows a devaluation. Sweden raises interest rates.
Sept 10, 1992 -. British Prime Minister John Major rules out devaluation within ERM as "a betrayal of our future."
Sept 13, 1992 - First major realignment of the ERM since January 1987 as behind-the-scenes deal brings seven per cent devaluation of the lira in return for a cut in German interest rates.
Sept 14, 1992 - Bundesbank announces quarter-point cut in Lombard rate and half point cut in discount rate. Markets unfazed and pressure on pound and lira resumes.

Sept 16, 1992 - "Black Wednesday." Markets attack pound, lira and peseta, forcing them below ERM floors. Central banks intervene and Britain announces unprecedented two-stage rise in base rate from 10 to 15 percent and then suspends pound from ERM. Pound effectively devalued, rates reduces rate to 12 percent. Swedish overnight rate to 500 percent.
Sept 17, 1992 - After a six-hour meeting, EC's monetary committee suspends lira from ERM. Peseta devalued by five percent and Britain cuts reduces base rate to 10 percent.
Sept 20, 1992 - French voters approve Maastricht treaty, with 51.05 percent in favour, but result doesn't prevent further pressure on ERM currencies.

Sept 23, 1992 - France and Germany launch counter-offensive against currency speculation that threatens to blow ERM apart. They appear to hold the line and markets calm down. Exchange controls imposed temporarily in Ireland, Spain and Portugal.
Nov 19, 1992 - Sweden abandons efforts to peg crown to the European currency unit, sparking new turmoil.
Nov 22, 1992 - Portugal and Spain devalue by six percent. Markets attack Irish punt, Danish crown and French franc.
Dec 12, 1992 - EC summit in Edinburgh reaffirms commitment to Maastricht treaty, saying ratification is needed for EC to remain anchor of stability in fast-changing continent.
Jan 1, 1993 - EU single market begins, temporary exchange controls lifted in Ireland, Spain and Portugal.
Jan 7, 1993 - Ireland raises overnight interest rates from 50 to 100 percent to fight off renewed speculation.
Jan 30, 1993 - Ireland devalues punt by 10 percent -- biggest single devaluation in 14 years of ERM.
Feb 1, 1993 - Market attention switches to Danish crown, but central bank intervention deflects it.
April 19, 1993 - EC finance ministers unveil 35 billion European currency unit ($42 billion) plan to boost faltering Community economies and create jobs.
May 13, 1993 - After two weeks of speculative pressure, peseta devalued by eight percent and escudo by 6.5 percent.
May 18, 1993 - Danes vote in favour of Maastricht treaty at second referendum, but vote fails to quash speculation that the move to EC monetary union is off the rails.
June 21, 1993 - French intervention rate falls below German discount for first time in 23 years.
June 21/22, 1993 - EC summit in Copenhagen launches major review of labour market and strategies for growth, and calls for quick cuts in European interest rates.
July 12, 1993 - Bundesbank intervenes to buy French francs.
July 29, 1993 - Bundesbank ignores market speculation it will cut its discount rate to save the ERM, leaves the rate untouched and shaves half a point off less important Lombard.
July 30, 1993 - Selling continues, pushing French franc through ERM floor several times. Central banks intervene.

Aug 1, 1993 - EU Monetary Committee hands proposals to an emergency session of EC finance ministers and central bank governors. After 12 hours of talks, early in the morning of Aug 2 they announce a major reshaping of the ERM, allowing all its currencies except the German mark and Dutch guilder to fluctuate by 15 percent above and below their central rates. The mark and guilder maintain a 2.25 percent range.
Nov 1, 1993 - German constitutional court rules in favour of Maastricht Treaty.
Jan 1, 1994, - Stage Two of EMU formally begins, European Monetary Institute founded in Frankfurt.
Sept 6, 1994 - Germany's ruling CDU party issues proposal for two-speed Europe, with inner-core going to EMU in 1999.
Oct 17, 1994 - Germany's Chancellor Kohl wins fourth term.
Jan 8, 1995 - Austrian schilling joins the ERM with 15 percent fluctuation bands at a central rate of 13.7167 schillings per Ecu and 14.2136 marks per 100 schillings.
March 6, 1995 - Spanish peseta devalued 7.0 percent and Portuguese escudo devalued 3.5 percent.
May 8, 1995 - Jacues Chirac elected French president.
Dec 15, 1995 - EU leaders confirm Jan, 1, 1999 as start date for single currency.
Oct 14, 1996 - Finland joins the ERM with 15 percent fluctution bands at a central rate of 5.80661 markka per Ecu and 3.04 markka to the mark.
Nov 25, 1996 - Italy rejoins ERM after four years of absence with 15 percent fluctuation bands at a central rate of 1906.48 per ECU and 990 lire to the mark.
